eigenmietwert.definition: A notional 'rent' the Swiss tax system adds to your taxable income for living in your own home. You pay income tax on it, but can deduct mortgage interest and maintenance costs. Swiss voters approved abolishing it in 2025, though the timing still varies by canton.

tragbarkeit.definition: The Swiss affordability test a bank applies before lending. Your modelled annual housing costs — interest at a notional 5% rate, amortisation and about 1% maintenance — must stay under one third of your gross income.

belehnungswert.definition: The value a bank actually lends against, which can be lower than the price you pay. Banks use the lower of the purchase price and their own valuation, so any gap between them must be covered with your own cash.

minergie.definition: A Swiss sustainability standard for low-energy buildings. Minergie-certified homes cost more to build but use far less energy and tend to hold their resale value better; some banks offer more favourable mortgage terms for them.

gebaeudeprogramm.definition: A joint federal and cantonal subsidy programme that pays toward energy renovations such as insulation, heat pumps and solar. The amounts and rules vary by canton, and you usually have to apply before starting the work.

pillar2.definition: Your occupational pension fund. You can withdraw or pledge part of it toward buying a home, but it counts as 'soft' equity — at least 10% of the price must still come from genuine cash savings.

amortisation.definition: Gradually paying down your mortgage. Swiss rules require the portion above roughly 67% of the property's value (the 'second mortgage') to be repaid within 15 years, or by the time you reach retirement.

niederstwertprinzip.definition: The 'lowest-value principle': a bank lends against the lower of the purchase price and its own valuation. If you pay more than the bank's assessed value, you have to fund the difference yourself in cash.

geak.definition: The Gebäudeenergieausweis der Kantone rates a building's energy performance from A (best) to G (worst). The class directly predicts your heating costs and signals whether an energy renovation is worth it.

solidarschuldnerschaft.definition: Joint and several liability. When two people take a mortgage together, each is fully liable for the entire debt — not just their half. If one cannot pay, the bank can pursue the other for the full amount.

liquid_cash.definition: Money you can use right away: checking and savings accounts, and investments you can sell quickly without a penalty. Retirement accounts usually don’t count, and it’s wise to keep an emergency fund on top of what you plan to spend on buying.

down_payment.definition: The part of the price you pay yourself; the mortgage covers the rest. A bigger down payment means a smaller loan and lower monthly costs. In the US first-time buyers can put as little as 3% down; in Switzerland the minimum is 20%.

closing_costs.definition: One-time fees you pay when you buy: lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, recording fees and prepaid taxes and insurance. They usually add up to about 2–5% of the price, on top of the down payment.

pmi.definition: Insurance that protects the lender when you put less than 20% down. You pay it monthly, usually about 0.3–1.5% of the loan a year. You can ask to cancel it once you owe 80% of the original price, and it ends automatically at 78%.

debt_to_income.definition: Your monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income. Lenders look at housing costs alone (a guideline of 28%) and housing plus other debts like car and student loans (36% as a comfortable guideline; some lenders go to 45–50%).

loan_estimate.definition: A standard 3-page form every lender must give you within 3 business days of applying. Because it has the same layout everywhere, you can compare offers line by line: rate, points, fees and closing costs.

preapproval.definition: A lender checks your income, debts, credit and savings and states how much it would likely lend you. It shows sellers you’re a serious buyer. It isn’t a final loan approval.

mortgage_rate_vs_apr.definition: The interest rate sets your monthly payment. The APR adds lender fees and points, spread over the loan, so it’s a better way to compare total cost between offers. Your actual rate depends on your credit score, down payment and the lender.

conforming_loan.definition: A conforming loan is small enough for Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac to buy ($832,750 in most counties in 2026). Bigger loans are “jumbo” loans, which usually need a higher credit score, more cash in reserve, and sometimes a higher rate.

piti.definition: Principal, interest, taxes and insurance: the four parts of a typical monthly mortgage payment. Add mortgage insurance and HOA dues if you have them. Lenders use this total for the 28% housing-cost test.

property_tax.definition: A yearly local tax on the value of your home, set by your county or city. It varies a lot: from about 0.5% of the value a year in some states to nearly 2% in others. It’s usually paid monthly through your mortgage.

homeowners_insurance.definition: Insurance on the house and your belongings against damage like fire or storms, plus liability. Lenders require it. Floods and earthquakes usually need separate cover.

hoa_fees.definition: Monthly fees to a homeowners association, common for condos and many newer neighborhoods. They pay for shared areas and services. Lenders count them in your housing costs.

amortization.definition: Paying a loan off gradually. With a 30-year fixed mortgage each payment is the same, but early on most of it is interest; over time more goes to the balance until it reaches zero.

home_equity.definition: The part of your home you actually own: its value minus what you still owe on the mortgage. It grows as you pay down the loan and if the home’s value rises.

down_payment_assistance.definition: Help from state or local programs, often as a grant or a low- or no-interest second loan, to cover part of the down payment or closing costs. Most have income and price limits and require a homebuyer class.

area_median_income.definition: The middle household income for your area, published by HUD. Many assistance and rebate programs are limited to households at or below a share of it, for example 80% or 150% of AMI.

housing_counselor.definition: A free or low-cost advisor at a nonprofit approved by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. They help with budgets, credit and assistance programs, and they don’t sell you a loan.

hers_index.definition: An energy rating for homes from a certified rater. 100 means a home built to 2006 code; lower is better, and 0 means the home makes as much energy as it uses. A typical existing home scores about 130; new homes average about 53.

energy_star_homes.definition: A new home independently checked to be at least 10% (typically about 20%) more efficient than homes built to code, with better insulation, windows, heating and cooling.

heat_pump.definition: An electric system that moves heat instead of making it, so it heats in winter and cools in summer. It uses far less energy than electric heating; whether it beats a gas furnace on cost depends on local electricity and gas prices.

net_metering.definition: How your utility credits the solar power you send back to the grid. With full net metering you get the retail rate; under newer rules like California’s net billing, exports earn much less, so using your own power matters more.

hard_equity.definition: The part of your down payment that must come from your own cash or Pillar 3a, not your pension fund. Swiss banks want at least 10% of the price as hard equity.

pillar3a.definition: A tax-advantaged private retirement account. You can deduct yearly contributions (up to CHF 7,258 for employees with a pension fund in 2026) from taxable income, and you can use it toward buying your own home.

notional_rate.definition: The deliberately high interest rate (5%) Swiss banks use to test whether you could still afford the home if rates rose. It isn’t the rate you’d actually pay.

mortgage_types_ch.definition: A fixed-rate mortgage locks the rate for a set term, often 5–10 years. A SARON mortgage follows the Swiss reference rate and changes every few months, so it’s cheaper when rates are low but less predictable.

property_appreciation.definition: How much a home’s value rises each year. It varies a lot by area and over time, and values can also fall. In Compare it’s your own guess for the future, not a forecast.

investment_return.definition: How much money you invest grows each year, for example in a broad stock index fund. Long-run averages have been a few percent a year after inflation, but returns swing from year to year and aren’t guaranteed.

rent_inflation.definition: How much your rent goes up each year. Over many years even small yearly increases add up, which is one reason buying can come out ahead in the long run.

opportunity_cost.definition: What you give up by choosing one option over another. Money tied up in a down payment can’t grow in investments at the same time; Compare’s “true cost” view adds that missed growth.

break_even.definition: The year when two choices, like renting and buying, leave you equally well off. Before it one is ahead; after it the other is.

net_worth.definition: Everything you own minus everything you owe. In Compare it’s your invested savings plus your home equity after selling costs.
